title: Two Houses, Two Feasts
summary: Wisdom builds a house with seven pillars, prepares a banquet of meat and mixed wine, and sends her servants to invite the simple to leave folly and live. A short interlude contrasts the mocker, who hates correction, with the wise, who grow wiser when rebuked, and repeats that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Then Folly, loud and ignorant, calls to the same passers-by from her doorway, promising that stolen water is sweet; but her guests are in the depths of Sheol.
story: Proverbs 9 brings the book's opening section to its climax. Since chapter 1, the young reader has heard two sets of voices: the father and Wisdom on one side, the violent gang and the forbidden woman on the other. Here the choice is staged as two rival banquets, set up in the same public space and addressed to the same simple passers-by with almost identical words. After this chapter, the book turns to the collections of individual sayings beginning in chapter 10. Chapter 9 is the doorway: the reader must accept Wisdom's invitation before the sayings that follow can do their work.
historical:
The chapter has no historical setting of its own and belongs with the rest of chapters 1 to 9 in date. Its picture of a great house with a banquet, servants, and invitations reflects the customs of wealthy households and royal courts in the ancient Near East. In several ancient Near Eastern texts, a god or goddess celebrates the completion of a house or temple with a feast, and some scholars see an echo of that pattern here, with Wisdom's house as a kind of temple or even the ordered world itself. Others read it more simply as the house of a noble lady hosting a banquet.

The seven pillars of verse 1 have been interpreted in many ways: as a sign of a large and well-built house, since ordinary houses had few pillars; as the number of completeness, meaning a perfect house; as the pillars of the world in ancient cosmology; or, in later Jewish and Christian allegory, as the days of creation, the books of the law, or the gifts of the Spirit. The text does not explain the number, and it is wise not to build much on it.
cultural:
Meat was a luxury in ancient Israel, eaten mostly at festivals, sacrifices, and special occasions, so slaughtering animals for a banquet signaled a generous host and a great occasion. Wine was often mixed with water or with spices; mixing wine was part of preparing a proper feast. Sending out servant girls to call guests from the high places of the city was how a wealthy host would issue invitations. Wisdom's banquet is lavish and public.

Folly's setup looks similar but is cheaper and more furtive. She sits at her own door, calls from a seat in the heights, and offers not a prepared feast but stolen water and bread eaten in secret. In a land where water was carefully owned and guarded (see 5:15-16), stolen water meant pleasure taken from what belongs to someone else, most likely another man's wife. The thrill of the forbidden is the whole of her offer. The dead in her house, called by the same word used in 2:18, rephaim, are the shades of Sheol.
literary: The chapter is built in three panels. Verses 1 to 6 describe Wisdom's house and invitation; verses 13 to 18 describe Folly's, deliberately matching it. Both women sit or call from the heights of the city, and both use the same words in verses 4 and 16: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” The difference lies in what follows. Wisdom offers bread, wine, life, and understanding; Folly offers stolen pleasure and death. Between the two panels stands a middle section (verses 7 to 12) of wisdom sayings on correcting mockers and teaching the wise, centered on verse 10, which repeats and echoes the motto of 1:7. The repetition frames the whole section of chapters 1 to 9: it begins and ends with the fear of the LORD.

outline.t: Wisdom's house and banquet: come and live
The mocker, the wise, and the fear of the LORD
Folly's invitation: stolen water and the depths of Sheol

doctrines.note: Verse 10 restates the foundation of the book: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowing the Holy One is understanding. Wisdom is finally not a technique but a relationship with the holy God.
The title the Holy One (verse 10) names God as utterly set apart, pure, and other. True understanding begins with knowing him as holy, not with knowing about the world.
Wisdom's invitation is to leave folly behind and walk in the way of understanding (verse 6). Turning in to her house means turning away from one road and onto another, the basic shape of repentance.

words.note: Yirah, fear. The fear of the LORD, repeated here from 1:7, is reverent awe that shows itself in trust and obedience. Its placement at the heart of chapter 9 and at the start of chapter 1 frames the entire opening section. Everything the father has taught grows from this root.

Luts, to mock or scoff. The mocker (lets) is the hardest case in Proverbs: not merely naive or foolish but actively contemptuous of correction. Verses 7 and 8 advise that rebuking a mocker only brings insult, while rebuking a wise person wins his love. The way someone receives correction reveals what they are.

Qadosh, holy. The word describes what is set apart and belongs to God, and when used of God it names his supreme, pure otherness. In verse 10 it appears as a title, the Holy One, parallel to the LORD. Isaiah's favorite name for God is the Holy One of Israel.

christ: Jesus often described the kingdom of God as a banquet to which invitations go out, and in his parable of the wedding feast a king sends out servants to call guests, and when the first refuse, the invitation goes to the streets (Matthew 22:1-10; Luke 14:16-24). The pattern is close to Wisdom's feast, though Jesus doesn't cite this chapter. In John 6 Jesus calls himself the bread of life, offering himself as food that gives eternal life. Christians have long read Wisdom's invitation to eat her bread and drink her wine (verse 5) alongside the Lord's Supper, though this is an application rather than the chapter's original meaning. The two feasts of Proverbs 9 anticipate the New Testament's picture of two ways: the narrow way that leads to life and the broad way that leads to destruction (Matthew 7:13-14).

hard.q: Does verse 11 promise a longer life to everyone who is wise?
hard.a: Verse 11 says that through wisdom your days will be multiplied and years added to your life. Like similar promises in chapters 3 and 4, this is a proverb describing how life tends to go, not a guarantee for every individual. Wise living does tend to protect people from violence, recklessness, addiction, and many dangers that shorten lives, and the book's opening chapters have shown folly leading to early death. But Scripture also records wise and righteous people who died young, and the book of Ecclesiastes says plainly that the same fate comes to the wise and the foolish (Ecclesiastes 2:14-16). The Old Testament's hope that the righteous will truly live finds its fullest answer in the resurrection, which the New Testament proclaims. Read as a promise that the faithful will never die early, the verse would be cruel to grieving families; read as a proverb, it is a true description of the direction wisdom takes a life.

questions: Wisdom and Folly use the same words of invitation. How can you tell the difference between them when both sound appealing?
Why do you think stolen water tastes sweet? What makes forbidden things feel more attractive than good ones?
Verses 8 and 9 say the wise love those who correct them. How do you usually respond to rebuke, and what does that reveal?
